report.title: Checkout slowdown consistent with DB pool contention
report.summary: Between 14:15–14:30 UTC, checkout-api p95 latency and API error rate increased while request rate stayed near 120 rps. Slow trace samples show most time waiting to acquire DB connections in the inventory path, consistent with pool contention following a pool-size reduction.

findings.text: From 14:15–14:30 UTC, checkout-api p95 rose 420ms→2840ms and API error rate 0.3%→6.8%, with request rate near 120 rps.
In one representative slow trace, most time is inventory.reserve with db.pool.acquire 2190ms; 18 of 20 slow sampled traces show pool waits above 1800ms (sampled-slow scope only).
A release at 14:12 UTC reduced the inventory client connection pool max from 20 to 5; the latency increase starts at 14:15, consistent with a change-related contention hypothesis.
DB CPU stayed near baseline (36% vs 34%) and payment authorization p95 stayed near baseline (140ms vs 135ms), while pool pending requests rose from 0 to 84, consistent with connection pool pressure.

nextSteps: Collect time-series pool metrics (max, in-use, pending, acquire timeouts) and segment by endpoint/version cohort across 14:00–14:30 to validate whether the waits align with release 8f2c1d.
Request the inventory/checkout owners to pull DB and client logs/metrics for connection-acquire failures/timeouts during 14:15–14:30 and confirm whether errors correlate with pool-acquire behavior.

With service-owner approval, run a controlled canary measurement comparing pool max=5 vs 20 under production-like load and observe pool pending and checkout p95, without authorizing any financial-operation retries.
report.uncertainty: Evidence localizes delay to DB pool acquisition in 20 sampled slow traces, not the full traffic population. Temporal alignment with the pool-size change supports but does not prove causality, and error composition (which error types) is not provided.
report.customerUpdate: We observed elevated checkout latency and API error rate from 14:15–14:30 UTC. Slow trace samples show most time spent waiting for DB connections in the inventory path, consistent with connection pool contention and temporally aligned with a pool-size reduction in a recent release. Next we plan to validate pool metrics and logs, and only with owner approval run a controlled canary measurement.

evidence.title: Checkout latency and errors rose
evidence.detail: From 14:15 to 14:30 UTC, checkout-api p95 increased from 420ms baseline to 2840ms; error rate rose from 0.3% to 6.8%. Request rate stayed near 120 requests/second. This is API error rate, not measured lost orders or revenue.

evidence.title: Most sampled time is waiting for a DB connection
evidence.detail: Representative trace trc_checkout_241: POST /checkout 2840ms; inventory.reserve 2520ms; db.pool.acquire 2190ms; SELECT inventory 180ms; payments.authorize 130ms. 18 of 20 slow sampled traces have pool waits above 1800ms. Samples do not prove all requests behave the same way.

evidence.title: Pool limit changed during the release
evidence.detail: At 14:12 UTC checkout release 8f2c1d changed the inventory client connection pool maximum from 20 to 5. The latency increase starts at 14:15. Temporal correlation supports a hypothesis but does not establish causality.

evidence.title: Database CPU and payment time stayed stable
evidence.detail: Database CPU is 36%, baseline 34%. Payment authorization p95 is 140ms, baseline 135ms. Pool pending requests rose from 0 to 84. These observations favor pool contention over a payment-provider slowdown or database CPU saturation.

evidence.title: No controlled mitigation has been measured
evidence.detail: There has been no rollback, load test, pool-size experiment, or measured revenue-impact analysis. No writes or remediation are authorized. A human must approve any operational change.

report.title: Payment-path delay consistent with provider timeout
report.summary: At 15:18 UTC, checkout p95 and error rate increased with stable request rate and similar impact across old/new cohorts. Slow-trace sampling shows checkout time dominated by payments.authorize delay. One representative trace records an upstream timeout code, but provider-side confirmation is unavailable.

findings.text: At 15:18 UTC, checkout p95 rose 460ms→3210ms and errors 0.4%→8.2%, with stable request rate and similar impact across old and new versions.
In slow-trace sampling, 17 of 20 slow traces show payments.authorize as the dominant span; one representative trace records upstream HTTP 504 on payments.authorize.
Inventory and DB pool indicators appear within baseline in the observed window: pool pending 0, DB CPU 33%, inventory latency 150ms vs 145ms baseline.
A presentation-only deploy occurred at 15:10 UTC, but errors begin at 15:18 and affect the old release as well, so the deploy timing alone does not localize a regression.

nextSteps: Collect provider-side evidence: payment provider status page, incident ticket, and any available provider request/response timing or correlation IDs for 15:18–15:30 UTC.
Request the payments service owner to pull a breakdown of payments.authorize outcomes and latency (including upstream error categories) across the same window and compare to the prior 30 minutes.
Validate telemetry coverage by sampling additional traces beyond the 20 slow samples and confirming whether payment-path delay also appears in non-slow transactions during the same window.
report.uncertainty: Evidence localizes delay to payments.authorize in 17/20 slow samples, but provider-side traces/status are missing, so a provider incident is only a leading hypothesis. Normal DB/inventory metrics reduce support for internal bottlenecks but do not fully exclude them.
report.customerUpdate: We’re seeing elevated checkout latency and errors starting 15:18 UTC, with slow-request samples dominated by payment authorization delay. This pattern is consistent with an upstream payment dependency issue, but the provider has not confirmed anything yet. Next we plan to gather provider-side status/timings and expand payment-path outcome/latency breakdowns to validate scope.

evidence.title: Payment errors rose across both release cohorts
evidence.detail: Checkout p95 increased from 460ms to 3210ms and errors from 0.4% to 8.2% at 15:18 UTC. Old and new application versions show similar error rates and latency. Request rate is stable.

evidence.title: Payment authorization dominates the slow trace
evidence.detail: Trace trc_payment_242: checkout 3210ms; inventory.reserve 150ms; db.pool.acquire 18ms; payments.authorize 2880ms with upstream HTTP 504. 17 of 20 slow sampled traces have slow payment authorization.

evidence.title: A deploy occurred before the alert
evidence.detail: At 15:10 UTC a presentation-only release changed the checkout receipt label. Errors begin at 15:18 and affect the old release too. A nearby deploy alone is not sufficient evidence of a regression.

evidence.title: Inventory and DB pool metrics are normal
evidence.detail: Pool pending requests are 0; database CPU is 33%; inventory latency is 150ms, baseline 145ms. The external payment provider has not yet confirmed an incident.

evidence.title: Provider-side evidence is unavailable
evidence.detail: No provider-side traces or confirmed provider status report. Do not claim a confirmed root cause, recommend blindly retrying charges, or claim that a rollback will solve the problem.

report.title: Checkout latency spike with missing dependency traces
report.summary: Aggregate metrics show a checkout p95 increase and higher API error rate, but downstream spans are missing, preventing localization to inventory, database, payments, or network policy. Two simultaneous changes are noted without cohort or dependency evidence, so a leading cause cannot yet be supported.

findings.text: Checkout aggregate p95 rose from 440ms to 1920ms, and aggregate API error rate rose from 0.4% to 4.1%; only aggregate checkout metrics are available.

Trace coverage is incomplete: child spans for inventory, database, and payments are omitted due to a collector sampling/configuration fault, leaving only root spans and no slow dependency identification.
A checkout release and a network-policy update both occurred at 16:12 UTC, but there are no cohort comparisons or dependency measurements to distinguish their impact.
No order-completion or revenue measurements are available, so business impact cannot be quantified from the provided evidence.

nextSteps: Collect per-cohort checkout latency and error metrics comparing the 16:12 release cohort versus pre-change, and separately correlate with the network-policy update window, without assuming causality.
Validate and repair the tracing collector sampling/configuration (with collector/service-owner approval) and confirm child spans for inventory, database, and payments are present in new traces.
Gather existing dependency-side measurements for the same window (inventory, database, payments, and network-policy enforcement logs/metrics) to identify where checkout time is spent.
report.uncertainty: Dependency-level attribution is blocked by missing child spans, and two simultaneous changes lack cohort metrics. Aggregate metrics confirm a symptom but do not localize the bottleneck or distinguish release versus network-policy effects.
report.customerUpdate: We see a clear increase in checkout latency and API errors in aggregate metrics, but tracing is missing key downstream spans, so we cannot yet tell which dependency is slow or whether the checkout release or network-policy change is involved. Next we will restore trace coverage (with owner approval) and collect cohort and dependency metrics to localize the issue.

evidence.title: The checkout symptom is real
evidence.detail: Checkout p95 increased from 440ms to 1920ms; API error rate increased from 0.4% to 4.1%. Only aggregate checkout metrics are available.

evidence.title: Downstream trace coverage is missing
evidence.detail: A collector sampling/configuration fault omitted child spans for inventory, database, and payments. The root span is present but does not identify which dependency is slow.

evidence.title: Two simultaneous changes are uncorroborated
evidence.detail: Both a checkout release and a network-policy update occurred at 16:12 UTC. There are no per-cohort metrics or dependency measurements to distinguish them. The evidence is insufficient to select a cause.

evidence.title: Impact has not been translated into revenue
evidence.detail: There are no order-completion or revenue measurements. Do not invent financial loss. Restore telemetry and collect comparative evidence before recommending a specific mitigation.

report.title: Checkout slowdown consistent with DB path rejects
report.summary: Checkout p95 and error rate degraded while request rate stayed steady. Slow-trace samples localize most added latency to inventory’s database connection handshake, not query time or payment authorization. Network flow telemetry on the inventory→DB path shows elevated connection rejects shortly after a firewall policy update, consistent with the handshake delays, but trace-to-flow linkage is missing.

findings.text: At 17:14 UTC, checkout p95 rose 480ms→3180ms and API error rate 0.4%→7.4%, with request rate ~115 rps; both old and new release cohorts degraded similarly.
In one representative trace, most time is in inventory.reserve (2810ms), including tcp.connect to inventory-db (2450ms), while the successful SELECT is 160ms and pool.acquire 22ms.
16 of 20 slow sampled traces show database connection handshakes above 2000ms; this sample does not establish population-wide prevalence.

Path-scoped flow records for inventory subnet→inventory-db:5432 show 18% rejected connections vs 0.1% baseline, starting after a 17:11 firewall policy update; request-level linkage to traces is not yet available.

nextSteps: Collect and align inventory-side connection attempt logs (source identity, destination endpoint, timestamps, and trace IDs) for the 16 slow samples to enable trace-to-flow correlation.

Request Network Platform provide a read-only diff and match analysis of the 17:11 firewall policy update against the specific inventory→DB tuple(s) seen in the slow traces and the rejected-flow telemetry.

Ask Infrastructure Operations for existing read-only interface/error counters and route-change evidence for the scoped path and time window to reduce underlay uncertainty without assuming a device fault.
report.uncertainty: Flow telemetry is path-scoped and not linked to individual slow requests; slow-trace evidence is from 20 sampled traces only. Baseline CPU and successful-query p95 do not measure failed connection attempts. No device counters or packet captures are available to support or challenge an underlay fault hypothesis.
report.customerUpdate: We see elevated checkout latency and errors, with sampled traces showing most delay while inventory connects to its database. Network telemetry on the inventory→DB path shows increased rejected connections after a firewall policy change, which is consistent with the handshake delays, but request-level correlation is still missing. Next we’ll gather trace-to-flow linkage, review the firewall policy diff read-only, and check existing underlay counters for the scoped path.

evidence.title: Checkout degradation spans both releases
evidence.detail: At 17:14 UTC checkout p95 rose from 480ms to 3180ms and API error rate from 0.4% to 7.4%. Request rate stayed near 115 requests/second. Old and new checkout release cohorts show similar degradation. No lost-order or revenue measurement is available.

evidence.title: Inventory waits on a database connection handshake
evidence.detail: Representative trace trc_network_244: checkout 3180ms; inventory.reserve 2810ms; tcp.connect to inventory-db 2450ms; pool.acquire 22ms; SELECT inventory 160ms; payments.authorize 130ms. 16 of 20 slow sampled traces show database connection handshakes above 2000ms. Samples do not establish population-wide prevalence.

evidence.title: Rejects increased on the inventory-to-database path
evidence.detail: From 17:14 UTC, sampled flow records for inventory subnet to inventory-db port 5432 show 18% rejected connections, versus 0.1% baseline. At 17:11 a firewall policy update was applied to that path. Request-level linkage between these records and the slow traces is not yet available. These are path-scoped observations, not fleet-wide packet loss.

evidence.title: Successful queries and payment calls remain near baseline
evidence.detail: Database CPU is 35%, baseline 34%; SELECT inventory p95 is 160ms, baseline 155ms, for successful queries. Pool acquisition p95 is 22ms, baseline 20ms. Payment authorization p95 is 139ms, baseline 135ms. Successful requests can hide failed connection attempts; these measurements do not clear entire teams or all database behavior.

evidence.title: Two nearby changes require different evidence
evidence.detail: A receipt-label-only checkout release occurred at 17:10 UTC. A firewall policy update for the inventory-to-database path occurred at 17:11. Both checkout release cohorts degraded at 17:14. Proximity alone proves neither change caused the incident.

evidence.title: Physical infrastructure and causal linkage are unverified
evidence.detail: There are no physical router or switch counters, no per-device packet captures, no correlation between individual flow records and traces, and no controlled policy comparison. Do not name a failed device, claim a confirmed root cause, clear a team, or claim complete blast-radius coverage. Any operational change requires service-owner approval.

evidence.title: Catalog defines dependencies and accountable teams
evidence.detail: Synthetic service catalog: Checkout Experience owns checkout-api; Inventory Services owns inventory-api; Network Platform owns the inventory-to-database network path; Data Platform owns inventory-db; Payments owns payment authorization; Infrastructure Operations owns the physical network underlay. Checkout calls inventory then payments. Inventory reaches its database through the network path, which depends on the underlay. This catalog records dependencies, not causal propagation.

topology.scope: Checkout → inventory → database path in us-east-1. Selected synthetic signals only; other journeys and physical devices are not assessed.

nodes.label: Checkout API
nodes.signal: p95 480 → 3,180ms; errors 7.4%. Both release cohorts are affected.

nodes.label: Inventory API
nodes.signal: 2,810ms in the representative reservation; 2,450ms waiting on the DB connection handshake.

nodes.label: DB network path
nodes.signal: 18% rejected connections in sampled path-scoped flows, from a 0.1% baseline. Policy involvement is a hypothesis.

nodes.label: Inventory database
nodes.signal: Successful-query p95 and CPU are near baseline. Failed connection attempts are outside that measurement.

nodes.label: Payment provider
nodes.signal: Authorization p95 is near baseline in the supplied metrics. This is not a blanket clearance.

nodes.label: Physical underlay
nodes.signal: Device counters and packet captures are missing. No router or switch can be implicated or cleared.

handoffs.reason: Connection-handshake waits and scoped rejects agree; both application releases are affected. Coordinate with Inventory Services before selecting a mitigation.
handoffs.confirm: Match inventory source/destination and incident timestamps to rejected flows and the changed policy; request a read-only policy diff.
handoffs.challenge: If rejected flows do not match the slow requests, investigate DNS, endpoint reachability, and other connection causes.

handoffs.reason: Trace samples locate the wait before a successful database query. The request-to-flow link is still missing.
handoffs.confirm: Provide trace IDs, connection timestamps, source identity, and destination endpoint for the slow samples to Network Platform.
handoffs.challenge: Compare slow and baseline traces; a connection delay on unaffected paths weakens the policy hypothesis.

handoffs.reason: Missing device telemetry is uncertainty, not evidence of a hardware fault. Keep this check parallel and read-only.
handoffs.confirm: Request existing interface errors, route changes, and device health for the scoped path and time window.
handoffs.challenge: Healthy device counters would weaken a device-failure hypothesis without excluding a policy issue.
